summary: A one-page announcement from Raj Reddy at Carnegie Mellon University about a one-day workshop on XCRIBL, a system for producing hard-copy line graphics. CMU had attached a Xerox graphic printer to its PDP-10 using a PDP-11 as a controller. The workshop was set for April 12, and the RFC gives contacts for details and local arrangements.

plainLanguage.summary: Carnegie Mellon connected a Xerox graphic printer to its computers and developed the XCRIBL system for producing text and images. RFC 320 announces a workshop about the system and lists its sessions.

subtitle: An announcement and program for a hard-copy graphics workshop

tldr.problem: The workshop notice introduces a system for producing hard-copy graphics and documents with a Xerox Graphic Printer.
tldr.mechanism: A PDP-11 controller connected the printer to a PDP-10 and generated image scan lines as needed.
tldr.outcome: Carnegie Mellon invited interested people to a workshop about XCRIBL and the supporting hardware and software.

today: RFC 320 describes Carnegie Mellon's XCRIBL printing setup and announces a workshop. Its account focuses on the system and the planned program for sharing information about it.

sections.title: The XCRIBL Printing System
sections.content:
Carnegie Mellon connected a Xerox Graphic Printer to a PDP-10 through a PDP-11 controller. Special hardware and data structures let the PDP-11 generate each scan line as needed, instead of first constructing a bit image for the whole page.

The notice says that the attached pages were produced by this system with document-generation and character-design programs.
sections.plainLanguage: The PDP-11 controller prepared the printer's image one scan line at a time. This avoided building a complete image of the page first.

sections.title: How the Printer Forms an Image
sections.content:
The XGP uses a cathode-ray tube to draw an image as dots. Light from the tube reaches a selenium drum, where exposed areas attract black powder. The powder transfers to paper and is fixed by a fuser.

A character-design program lets a user set or clear dots in a grid to create a character pattern. The printer can also draw lines and gray-scale images.
sections.plainLanguage: The printer draws dots on a tube, transfers the image to a drum and moves the resulting powder onto paper. Users can design character shapes by choosing their dots.

sections.title: Workshop Program
sections.content: The one-day workshop at Carnegie Mellon was scheduled for April 12. Its sessions covered XCRIBL, document-generation languages, examples of document production, character-set design, the PDP-11 support system and the printer interface. An evening discussion was planned for unresolved questions and possible hardware or software solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop covered the software, character design and hardware behind the printer. It also set aside time to discuss problems that still needed solutions.
